lesson.title: Factor of safety and sizing

steps.headline: Working stress and the factor of safety

lead.text: A tie is a bar that is pulled along its length, like the bottom chord of a truss. Last lesson you found the stress in such a bar, the force on each square millimetre of its cross-section. The stress it actually carries in use is its working stress, and the bar stays safe only while that is below the yield stress, the point where it stops springing back.

How far below is found by dividing one by the other. The factor of safety is the yield stress divided by the working stress. Take a tie of 200 mm² that carries 24 kN, in steel that yields at 360 MPa. Its working stress is 24,000 N ÷ 200 mm² = 120 MPa, so its factor of safety is 360 ÷ 120 = 3. The tie could take three times its working stress before it began to yield. The picture shows the same tie at two loads.

afterFigure.text: At 48 kN the same tie works at 240 MPa and the factor falls to 1.5. Doubling the load halves the factor, and a bar loaded right up to its yield stress has a factor of exactly 1.
The same ratio works with loads. For one bar, the load that would make it yield divided by the load it carries gives the same number, because the area cancels.

lead.text: Compare what the cable can take with what it is asked to take. The ratio from the last screen works on loads as well as stresses.
Find the working stress in MPa first, then compare it with the yield stress.

Once you can measure a margin, you have to decide how big it should be. The factor of safety covers everything that might make a bar weaker, or its load heavier, than the designer allowed for. A crowd or a gust of wind can arrive on top of the expected load. The steel can be a little weaker than its datasheet says, or lose some thickness to rust. The calculation itself can hold a mistake nobody has found.

The size of the margin follows from how well those things are known and what happens if they go wrong. Where the loads are known closely and weight matters a great deal, as in an aircraft, factors near 1.5 are used. Building frames use somewhat more, often around 2. A lift cable or a crane hook carries people or hangs over them, so it gets a much larger factor, because a failure there costs lives.
Whatever the factor, the designer fixes it first and lets it decide the size of the bar. The next screen shows how.

Turn the formula round. When the factor of safety is chosen in advance, the highest working stress you will permit is the yield stress divided by it. This is the allowable stress. Steel that yields at 300 MPa, used with a factor of 2, has an allowable stress of 300 ÷ 2 = 150 MPa.

The allowable stress answers two kinds of question. If you know the area, the largest load is the allowable stress times the area. A bar of 200 mm² can carry 150 N/mm² × 200 mm² = 30,000 N, which is 30 kN. If you know the load, the smallest area is the load divided by the allowable stress. A 42 kN load needs 42,000 N ÷ 150 N/mm² = 280 mm².
Keep the load in newtons and the stress in MPa and the area comes out in mm² with no further conversion.

steps.headline: A tie must carry 30 kN with a factor of safety of 2. The steel yields at 250 MPa. Find the least area.

lead.text: Here is the method from the last screen, written out line by line.

workedSteps.text: Divide the yield stress by the factor to get the allowable stress.
Area is the load in newtons over the allowable stress.

steps.headline: A tie must carry 60 kN with a factor of safety of 2, using steel that yields at 250 MPa. Find the least area.

lead.text: The method is the same as in the worked example.

workedSteps.text: Divide the yield stress by the factor to get the allowable stress.
Divide the load in newtons by the allowable stress, to get the area in mm².

lead.text: The area you calculate is a minimum, and mills do not make a bar of every size. A designer picks from a list, such as square bars with sides of 12 mm and 16 mm. The area of a square bar is its side squared, so these have 144 mm² and 256 mm².

Suppose a calculation asks for at least 200 mm², for a load of 25 kN at an allowable stress of 125 MPa. The 12 mm bar is too small. It would work at 25,000 ÷ 144, about 174 MPa, which is above the 125 MPa allowed. The 16 mm bar works at about 98 MPa, so it is the smallest bar that passes. The picture shows both.

afterFigure.text: Rounding up leaves a factor of safety a little above the one you chose, which is the safe direction. Rounding down never is, so you take the smallest bar whose area is at least what the calculation gave.

lead.text: Work out the area of each bar in turn and drop any that is too small. Then take the smallest one left.

steps.headline: Strong enough is not always stiff enough

lead.text: A bar can pass every strength check and still be a poor tie, because it also stretches. If the tie holds something that must stay in line, the stretch can matter as much as the strength. You found the stretch of a loaded bar last lesson: strain is the stress divided by E, and the stretch is the strain times the original length.

Take a steel tie of 400 mm² and 4 m length, carrying 30 kN. Its stress is 30,000 ÷ 400 = 75 MPa. With E = 200,000 MPa the strain is 75 ÷ 200,000 = 0.000375, and over 4,000 mm that is a stretch of 0.000375 × 4,000 = 1.5 mm.

Whether 1.5 mm is acceptable depends on the job. A roof tie can usually take it, and a rod that holds a machine in line cannot. When the stretch sets the limit, the bar is chosen to meet it, and the factor of safety ends up higher than the design needed.
The tie in this question passes the strength check. This time the question is how far it stretches. Use E = 200,000 MPa.

lesson.orientation: Size a member for strength with a margin, then check that it is stiff enough.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: The last lesson followed a steel rod as its load grew, up to the stress where it stops springing back. Nobody loads a bar that far on purpose. A lift cable can carry a load many times heavier than any lift will put on it, and the bolts in a bridge and the chain on a crane hook are chosen the same way.

That spare strength is deliberate, and it has a price, because a stronger part is thicker, heavier and dearer. With too little spare strength, one bad day brings the structure down. With too much, the design wastes material or becomes too heavy to lift into place.

This lesson follows one steel tie, a bar that is pulled along its length. We measure how much spare strength it has and decide how much it should have. That choice sets the size of the tie, and a last check shows whether a bar strong enough also stretches too far.

intro.promise: By the end you'll size a steel member from a factor of safety, and check that it does not stretch too much.

recap.keyIdea: The factor of safety is the yield stress divided by the working stress. To size a member, divide the yield stress by the factor to get the allowable stress, then find the area and check the stretch.

blocks.text: The cable that holds five times its load has a factor of safety of 5. For the steel tie you found a factor of 2.5 at 40 kN on 400 mm². You then sized a tie for 60 kN at a factor of 2, which needed 480 mm² and so the 25 mm square bar. That bar stretches 1.44 mm over 3 m, so strength and stiffness are separate checks.

recap.nextHook: Every bar so far was pulled straight along its length. A beam carries loads across it, and the next lesson cuts one in half to see what holds each piece in place.

questions.prompt: A lift cable would snap under 100 kN, but it only ever carries 20 kN. How many times stronger is the cable than it needs to be?
hints: What would you divide to compare the strength with the load?
How many times does 20 go into 100?
Count in twenties up to one hundred.
questions.onCorrect: 5 times: strength divided by load. For a single bar, that ratio is its factor of safety.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the gap between them. The question asks how many times larger, which is a ratio.
That is the load over the strength, upside down. The cable is stronger than the load.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The cable can take 100 kN and carries 20 kN, so it is 100 ÷ 20 = 5 times stronger than needed.

questions.prompt: Bar A yields at 300 MPa and works at 100 MPa. Bar B yields at 300 MPa and works at 150 MPa. Which has the larger factor of safety?
hints: Divide the yield stress by the working stress for each bar.
questions.onCorrect: Bar A's factor is higher: the same yield stress divided by a smaller working stress.

misconceptions.feedback: A higher working stress leaves less margin, so the factor is smaller.
The yield stresses match, but the working stresses differ, so the factors do too.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Bar A. Dividing 300 by each working stress gives 3 for the first bar and 2 for the second, so the first has the larger factor.

questions.prompt: A steel tie with yield stress 250 MPa and area 400 mm² carries 40 kN. Find its factor of safety against yield.
hints: Find the working stress first.
Divide the yield stress by the working stress.
questions.onCorrect: 2.5: the tie could take two and a half times its working stress before yielding.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the working stress. Compare it with the yield stress.
That is working stress over yield stress, upside down. The factor is more than one.

questions.prompt: Why is the allowable stress the yield stress divided by the factor of safety?
hints: What is the allowable stress meant to protect against?
questions.onCorrect: The allowable stress is the highest stress you permit: a safe fraction of the stress that fails the material.

misconceptions.feedback: A lower allowable stress needs more material, so the bar gets heavier, not lighter.
Stress is force per area. They are different quantities.

choices.label: It keeps the working stress a safe fraction of the stress that causes failure.
Because force and stress are the same thing.

acceptedIdeas: It keeps the working stress a safe fraction of the stress that causes failure.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It keeps the working stress a safe fraction of the stress that causes failure.. Dividing by the factor leaves the working stress a safe fraction of the failure stress.

hints: Area is load divided by allowable stress.
Use the load in newtons.
Calculate 60,000 ÷ 125.
questions.onCorrect: 480 mm²: the load in newtons over the allowable stress.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by the factor instead of dividing. The allowable stress is lower than yield.
That ignores the factor of safety. Divide the yield stress by it first.

questions.prompt: Square steel bars come with 20, 25 and 30 mm sides. Which side length, in mm, is the smallest that gives at least 480 mm² of area?
hints: Work out the area of each bar.
Discard any below the required area.
Pick the smallest remaining side.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Areas are 20 × 20 = 400, 25 × 25 = 625 and 30 × 30 = 900 mm². 400 mm² is too small, so the 25 mm bar is the lightest that works.

questions.onCorrect: 25 mm: the smallest stock bar that meets the area. Rounding up costs a little weight and gains margin.

misconceptions.feedback: That bar's area is below the area needed, so it would be overstressed.
That works, but it is heavier than needed. Choose the smallest bar that does.

questions.prompt: A 25 mm square steel tie (625 mm²) is 3 m long and carries 60 kN. With E = 200 GPa, find its stretch in mm.
hints: Find the stress in MPa.
Strain = stress ÷ 200,000 MPa; multiply by 3,000 mm.
questions.onCorrect: 1.44 mm. Safe against yield does not mean stiff enough: check the stretch against what the connection allows.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the stress in MPa. Divide by E and multiply by the length to get a stretch.

questions.prompt: A steel with yield stress 355 MPa is used with a factor of safety of 2.5. Find the allowable working stress in MPa.
hints: The factor of safety divides the failure stress.
Allowable = yield ÷ FoS.
Calculate 355 ÷ 2.5.
questions.onCorrect: 142 MPa: the yield stress divided by the factor of safety.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by the factor. The allowable stress is below yield, so divide.

questions.prompt: A 300 mm² bar of steel that yields at 250 MPa must keep a factor of safety of 1.5. Find the largest axial load it may carry, in kN.
hints: Find the allowable stress.
Load = allowable stress × area, in newtons.
Calculate 300 × 250 ÷ 1.5, then convert to kN.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Allowable stress = 250 ÷ 1.5 MPa; load = 300 × 250 ÷ 1.5 = 50,000 N = 50 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 50 kN: allowable stress times area, converted from newtons.

misconceptions.feedback: That ignores the factor of safety. The allowable stress is yield divided by it.
That is the load in newtons. The answer is wanted in kN.

questions.prompt: A bar of area 200 mm² carries 30 kN. Its steel yields at 240 MPa. Find its factor of safety against yield.
hints: Find the working stress in MPa.
Divide the yield stress by the working stress.
questions.onCorrect: 1.6: the yield stress is 1.6 times the working stress. That is a thin margin for most designs.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the working stress. Divide the yield stress by it.
That is working stress over yield stress, upside down.
